overview: The exact atlas record is labeled Wabanaki (Dawnland Confederacy) and spans 1492 to 1500, but its inherited summary describes a Maine child-welfare commission created in 2012. That summary belongs to another subject. Wabanaki means People of the Dawnland and is a collective name for related, distinct peoples, including Abenaki, Penobscot, Peskotomuhkati or Passamaquoddy, Wolastoqiyik, and Mi'kmaq nations. During these eight years there was no single centralized Wabanaki state with the painted polygon as a surveyed border. Nation and museum histories place formal Confederacy organization in the seventeenth century, while older kinship, exchange, diplomacy, and alliance networks had deep roots. Archaeology supports skilled life around rivers, lakes, coasts, and portages: fishing, hunting, gathering, pottery, bark technologies, storage, seasonal movement, and multi-season settlements. Evidence varies sharply by place, so Mi'kmaq, Penobscot, Wolastoqey, Peskotomuhkati, and Abenaki practices are attributed rather than merged. John Cabot's uncertain northern landfall in 1497 produced no documented Wabanaki encounter. Written-language sample: none securely attributable to this 1492 to 1500 Dawnland umbrella. At 1500 the atlas feature ends, while Wabanaki peoples, homelands, languages, and political life continue.

periods.title: 1492 to 1493: Dawnland life continues
periods.summary: The exact polygon begins in 1492, although the same id is absent in 1400. This is an atlas seam, not a founding event. Across Dawnland, distinct communities continued established water travel, food gathering, household work, kin relations, and exchange while Columbus sailed far south in the Caribbean.

periods.title: 1493 to 1494: distant claims do not create local rule
periods.summary: European religious and royal claims developed across the Atlantic without Wabanaki consent or occupation of Dawnland. No surviving local annual chronicle records a 1493 political change. Inhabited homelands, nation-specific leadership, and older intercommunity relationships matter more than paper claims made far away.

periods.title: 1494 to 1495: archaeology carries the evidence
periods.summary: For this year, pottery, hearths, food remains, tools, dwelling traces, and site locations provide stronger evidence than later narratives. Ceramic Period communities used canoe-navigable waters and could combine seasonal movement with multi-season settlement. Artifacts reveal activities more securely than personal names, beliefs, or exact political offices.

periods.title: 1495 to 1496: complexity without an invented council
periods.summary: Late Maritime Woodland evidence supports storage, aggregation, territorial relationships, substantial dwellings, and changing exchange. Those patterns correct stereotypes of politically simple wandering bands. They do not prove that one named pan-Wabanaki council met in 1495, or that every Dawnland community followed identical household and leadership arrangements.

periods.title: 1496 to 1497: waterways organize work and movement
periods.summary: Before Cabot's voyage, communities continued fishing, hunting, gathering, making pottery, maintaining shelters, and moving along coasts, rivers, lakes, and portages. Mi'kmaw Forillon evidence spans these years broadly, but no artifact can be assigned to this single year merely because its archaeological range overlaps it.

periods.title: 1497 to 1498: Cabot does not supply a meeting
periods.summary: Cabot reached an uncertain northern landfall, probably around Newfoundland, in 1497. His log is lost, surviving reports are secondhand, and accounts say he encountered no Indigenous people. This voyage cannot be turned into a first meeting, trade session, battle, or disease event with Wabanaki communities.

periods.title: 1498 to 1499: local continuity remains the honest account
periods.summary: Cabot's later expedition is poorly documented and supplies no secure annual event inside Dawnland. Families still needed to teach languages, routes, fishing, craft, food, and social responsibilities, yet the evidence does not preserve a dated lesson. Oral education and skilled practice are presented as continuities, not invented scenes.

periods.title: 1499 to 1500: an atlas ending opens a contact horizon
periods.summary: The exact feature disappears at 1500 and remains absent in 1530. That software change is not a Wabanaki collapse. Regular European fisheries, trade, epidemics, missions, colonial warfare, and formal Confederacy politics developed later, as newcomers entered an already longstanding Indigenous maritime world.

sections.title: People, names, and the atlas shape

items.text: The index has one exact id, wabanaki-dawnland-confederacy, dated approximately 1492 to 1500. Coverage finds one border feature and no finished card. These database facts identify an editorial task; they do not prove a confederate state began in 1492 or ended eight years later.

Wabanaki is commonly explained as People of the Dawnland. Related, distinct peoples include Abenaki, Penobscot, Peskotomuhkati or Passamaquoddy, Wolastoqiyik, and Mi'kmaq nations. A collective relationship does not erase each nation's homeland, language, living community history, political authority, or present sovereignty.

Separate atlas features for Abenaki, Penobscot, Mi'kma'ki, Passamaquoddy, and Wolastoqiyik overlap the Wabanaki artwork. Existing card and override records also keep similar ids distinct. This packet preserves those identities rather than treating the broad polygon as exclusive territory or a master record.

The imported two-part MultiPolygon has 296 positions and extends from parts of northern New England through the Maritimes. Its hard edges are display artwork, not surveyed fifteenth-century borders. Nation homelands, travel, family ties, and diplomatic relationships could cross the painted boundary or occupy overlapping space.

The inherited summary is about the Maine Wabanaki-State Child Welfare Truth and Reconciliation Commission, established in 2012 and reporting in 2015. It is important modern history, but it has no identity or chronological fit with this 1492 map layer and is replaced here.

Many known Ceramic Period sites cluster beside coasts, rivers, lakes, streams, and wetlands that canoes could navigate. Water linked food places, camps, villages, and exchange routes. Archaeological concentration also reflects where surveys and preservation occur, so a blank map area does not prove an empty homeland.

At Forillon, Indigenous presence from about 1000 to 1534 includes fire pits, domestic activity, stone-tool work, pottery used in fish cooking, and a portage corridor. This unusually useful date range overlaps 1492 to 1500, yet each activity still spans centuries rather than one exact year.

Ajemseg preserves a long Wolastoqey-country sequence whose archaeological phases include Ceramic or Maritime Woodland materials. The report supports enduring use of the Wolastoq watershed and careful local chronology. It does not make one excavated assemblage a complete portrait of every Wolastoqiyik household or all Dawnland.

Mi'kmaw canoe builders distinguish ocean-going craft from lake and river forms, adjusting hull, capacity, ribs, planking, bark, roots, pegs, gum sealant, and paddles to the water. Living expertise explains sophisticated engineering; archaeology and older records are still needed before assigning a particular construction detail to 1492.

Kouchibouguac lies within Mi'gma'ki and has twenty-six Indigenous archaeological sites across millennia. Its marine and inland resources supported seasonal economic and social life. That local coastal pattern should remain local: it cannot supply a fixed seafood percentage or seasonal calendar for interior Penobscot, Wolastoqey, or Abenaki communities.

A Peskotomuhkati-region site yielded more than three thousand fish remains, dominated by Atlantic tomcod with some herring. The study supports specialized fishing and seasonality in Passamaquoddy Bay. One rich catch does not become the menu of every Wabanaki nation, season, household, or inland settlement.

Mount Desert Island archaeology records hunting, fishing, shellfish gathering, ceramic cooking pots, bone and stone tools, and shell middens. Organic foods disappear more easily than shell and bone, so the surviving menu is incomplete. Archaeologists compare multiple traces rather than assuming that the largest midden held everyone's favorite meal.

The Carson Site is a major Passamaquoddy Bay shell-midden and Late Ceramic study, with evidence concerning fish, pottery, a housepit, seasonality, and settlement. Its older archaeological vocabulary needs newer Peskotomuhkati-centered context, while the site remains valuable for understanding one Quoddy-region place.

Mi'kmaq accounts describe hunting, fishing, plant gathering, seasonal locations, and knowledge of useful food and medicine plants. These nation-specific summaries show coordinated ecological knowledge. They do not justify a single Wabanaki recipe, crop list, harvest date, or division of food labor for every community in 1492.

Birchbark containers and baskets could carry or store food, while pitch helped seal and repair bark objects. A contemporary Penobscot practitioner describes bark selection, spruce-root sewing, and hands-on teaching. Such living knowledge demonstrates continuity and design skill, though it is not a verbatim fifteenth-century workshop manual.

Wikuom or wigwam forms used sapling frames, sewn birchbark panels, root or fiber lashings, and a central opening for smoke. Portability suited some seasonal movement. Museum objects and later descriptions explain construction principles, but no displayed nineteenth-century shelter should be relabeled as the exact house of a 1492 family.

Mi'kmaq clothing work included preparing hides, piercing with bone awls, and sewing with sinew. The same museum sheet describes portable bark-covered homes. Some details rely partly on seventeenth-century observation or cautious earlier inference, so they illuminate technical traditions without fixing every garment or household routine to this interval.

Port Joli dwelling floors reveal architecture, family occupation, and patterned use of space, while interpretation joins archaeology with later cultural knowledge. The best-dated features are earlier than 1492. They establish a deeper architectural history, not a license to reconstruct one universal late-fifteenth-century floor plan or rigid gender map.

Late Maritime Woodland research finds domestic architecture, storage, intensified food work, aggregation, territoriality, and exchange. These are substantial achievements by hunter-fisher-gatherer communities. The evidence also remains uneven, so complexity should be described through supported practices rather than converted into palaces, taxes, social ranks, or a regional capital.

Stone, bone, wood, bark, roots, hide, sinew, clay, and pitch required different chains of skilled work. Archaeology preserves fired clay and stone more readily than baskets, paddles, clothing, and wooden handles. Missing organic objects can distort a toolkit, so durable finds should not define all daily labor.

Museum accounts describe extended-family groups and nearby kin as central to home, work, teaching, and seasonal life. These sources approach 1492 through later records and continuity. They support the importance of relationships without proving one household size, marriage rule, residence pattern, or kin term across all nations.

Penobscot Nation presents women, mothers, and grandmothers as central family members, first teachers, keepers of oral knowledge, and advisers in recognizing leaders. This is Penobscot tradition and continuity. It should not be flattened into a universal job description assigned to every Wabanaki woman in 1492.

Penobscot curriculum materials connect nuclear, extended, community, and tribal relationships with homeland knowledge, oral tradition, and arts. Tribal specialists shaped the modern resources. They help explain living relational frameworks, while classroom exercises themselves are not primary evidence for one late-fifteenth-century household or lesson.

Mi'kmaq teaching summaries describe councils, elders, community responsibilities, seasonal territories, and systems of justice. Another government account identifies seven Mi'kmaq political districts under a Grand Council. These are Mi'kmaq national structures, not proof that a single pan-Wabanaki government ruled every Dawnland nation.

Consensus and respected leaders appear in accounts near 1600, and earlier communities aggregated for social and economic purposes. These clues support political skill without a centralized state. Leadership probably depended on relationships and persuasion, but exact offices and meetings for 1492 to 1500 are not securely documented.

Children learned within homes, work, travel, stories, and community relationships rather than from a surviving written school curriculum. Passamaquoddy museum material describes observation and productive tasks among nearby kin. It is a reconstruction informed by later evidence, so the card avoids invented ages, examinations, or a daily timetable.

Penobscot oral traditions are described as instructive as well as entertaining, carrying lessons about childhood, coming of age, landscape, and balance. The surviving tales were recorded much later. Their teaching role matters, but their recorded wording cannot be presented as a transcript of a story evening in 1492.

Abenaki snow snakes, birchbark toys, and dice show play joining material knowledge, coordination, strategy, and social time. Some described stakes and goods are post-contact, so they are excluded from exact-period claims. The responsible point is that children and adults learned through play, not that one game was universal.

Penobscot language lessons today include family, parents, grandparents, guests, feelings, and greetings in a distinct language. They demonstrate living teaching and continuity. Current spelling is not a 1492 inscription, and Penobscot cannot stand in as a common language spoken identically by every Wabanaki nation.

Children could be cherished, encouraged, cajoled, or teased, while stories and games could entertain as well as teach. That supports gentle, relational humor without preserving a datable joke. No punchline is invented here, and sacred characters are not reduced to comedy props for a modern audience.

Regional studies inventory plants and animals used for food and medicine, while Mi'kmaq summaries describe established plant knowledge. Many named remedies were recorded centuries later. They can show enduring expertise, but this card does not move a recipe, dosage, healer title, or promised medical effect backward into 1492.

A possible Maritime Woodland sweathouse demonstrates how archaeologists combine structure, heat effects, spatial evidence, and later accounts to test therapeutic or ritual interpretations. The feature is earlier than this card, and contemporary sweat ceremonies include later influences. It supports a long history of careful practice, not one exact ceremony.

Food security depended on detailed knowledge of seasons, waters, animals, plants, storage, travel, and cooperation. Those systems affected health even when bones do not preserve a diagnosis. A good history of medicine therefore includes nourishment and care while refusing to label particular diseases that exact-period evidence cannot demonstrate.

Bark selection, pitch sealing, hide preparation, smoke control, and food processing demanded attention to safe materials and working conditions. Sources document the techniques more securely than injuries or treatments. The card can describe preventive skill without inventing antiseptics, surgical methods, or a standardized Wabanaki clinic.

Health evidence differs by coast, estuary, island, river valley, season, and community. A specialized fishery, local shell midden, or plant list cannot become a regional nutrition score. Exact-period human remains are limited, so individual illness, disability, childbirth, recovery, and caregiving usually remain beyond secure reconstruction.

Water supported drinking, cooking, washing, food processing, travel, fishing, gathering, and ritual activity in tribally reviewed traditional-lifeways categories. That modern exposure model organizes evidence rather than replaying one ancient day. It cannot provide exact quantities, bathing frequency, water-treatment rules, or a shared 1492 sanitation code.

Settlements and camps often faced canoe-navigable water, linking movement and subsistence while providing access for everyday needs. Local sources, springs, river reaches, and coastal conditions varied. The reviewed evidence does not establish one Dawnland well design, pipe network, purification method, or household water allocation.

A roof opening let smoke leave bark-covered wikuom forms, although airflow also depended on fire, covering, weather, and maintenance. This is household engineering, not proof of a chimney in every dwelling. Later museum descriptions should clarify possibilities while remaining separate from an excavated 1492 structure.

Shell middens and refuse deposits preserve discarded food remains, broken pottery, and tools, allowing archaeologists to reconstruct activity and diet. A midden records disposal more readily than a rule about cleanliness. It does not prove municipal collection, household sweeping frequency, or where every category of waste went.

No securely attributable evidence in the reviewed sources identifies a Wabanaki toilet, latrine design, sewer, or fecal-waste routine in 1492 to 1500. Organic facilities and surface practices may leave little trace. The honest conclusion is limited evidence, not that people lacked privacy, hygiene, or designated places.

Late Maritime Woodland exchange moved stone and other materials across substantial distances, while aggregation brought communities together. Those networks required knowledge, trust, negotiation, and territorial relationships. They demonstrate organized power without requiring one monarch, tax system, capital, or hard border encompassing every place painted by the atlas.

Wolastoqey Nation describes older interregional structures underlying the Confederacy, but dates its formal establishment to the seventeenth century. That distinction is essential. Deep diplomacy and related peoples existed before Europeans, while a fully constituted Confederacy government should not be inserted into the eight years from 1492 to 1500.

Mi'kmaq political districts and Grand Council traditions show nation-level organization before European arrival. They belong to Mi'kmaq history and cannot be relabeled as offices of a pan-Wabanaki state. Comparing distinct political forms is more accurate than imagining Dawnland as politically empty or uniformly administered.

The Devil's Head site on the St. Croix River preserves both change and continuity between Late Maritime Woodland and protohistoric components. It cautions against a sudden 1492 rupture. European objects and later diplomatic pressures must follow their archaeological dates instead of being assigned automatically to this atlas interval.

No specific Confederacy-wide war is securely documented for 1492 to 1500 in the reviewed evidence. Conflict may have existed, but absence of a dated account prevents a battle narrative. Power is better shown through settlement, food systems, exchange, councils, alliances, expertise, and control of routes.

Kejimkujik preserves more than five hundred Mi'kmaw petroglyphs depicting people, canoes, clothing, signs, and later signatures across broad dates. They are sacred and vulnerable works in a living cultural landscape. Their presence supports visual expression, but an undated image cannot become a translated sentence from 1492.

A pre-contact eight-pointed motif in the Nova Scotia Museum catalogue adds evidence for Mi'kmaw visual systems. A recurring design can carry meaning without functioning as alphabetic prose. Its catalogue date and interpretation do not yield an author, spoken wording, or securely translatable language sample for these years.

Written-language sample: none securely attributable to this 1492 to 1500 Wabanaki and Dawnland umbrella. The documented Mi'kmaw missionary logographic system begins in 1677. Modern Penobscot spelling and the current Peskotomuhkati-Wolastoqey dictionary are valuable living resources, but neither is substituted for an interval-authored text.

The Abbe Museum cares for archaeological materials, baskets, bark containers, canoes, art, and archives spanning more than twelve thousand years. These collections demonstrate long Wabanaki creativity and survival, but their dates vary. Each object needs its own provenance before it can illustrate the late fifteenth century.

Passamaquoddy cultural work and collaborative language archives show living nations protecting knowledge after centuries of colonial disruption. The atlas feature vanishes in 1500, but Wabanaki people do not. Languages, governance, art, family ties, land relationships, scholarship, and cultural authority continue in distinct nations today.

ending.text: At 1500 the exact wabanaki-dawnland-confederacy feature disappears from the atlas, but no reviewed source identifies a matching collapse, conquest, depopulation, or end of Wabanaki political life. Later European fisheries, trade, epidemics, missions, warfare, and colonial dispossession brought profound change. Formal Confederacy organization belongs to the seventeenth century. Wabanaki nations, communities, languages, family relationships, knowledge, and responsibilities to Dawnland continue beyond the software boundary and into the present.
